title: Building a Sampling Distribution of p̂ — Medical Consultant

steps.instruction: Imagine a large bag of marbles: **10% orange** (complication) and **90% blue** (no complication). This bag models the world under **H₀**: the consultant's true complication rate matches the national **10%**. We can't see the whole bag in real life, but here we can — that's the **Population** panel, with the true proportion marked at **p = 0.10**. Each surgery is one draw from the bag; a "study" of **n = 62** surgeries is one scoop of 62 marbles, and the proportion of orange marbles in the scoop is one simulated **p̂** from the null distribution.
steps.observe: Find **p = 0.10** marked on the Population panel. Each scoop of 62 marbles will rarely be exactly 10% orange — that sample-to-sample wobble is what we're about to study.

steps.instruction: **Before you draw anything, commit to a prediction.** Imagine taking *hundreds* of scoops of 62 marbles and plotting each scoop's proportion orange (each one a simulated p̂ under H₀).

gate.question: Where will those sample proportions (p̂) pile up?

choices.feedback: You've committed — now draw samples and see whether the pile-up lands where you expected.
You've committed — draw samples and check. Watch where the center of the pile actually falls.
You've committed — draw samples and see whether the proportions really spread out evenly, or cluster somewhere.

steps.instruction: Click **+1** once. Watch the **One sample** panel show your scoop of 62 marbles, collapse to a single proportion **p̂**, and drop that one dot into the **Sampling distribution** panel at the bottom — one simulated study under H₀.
steps.observe: That bottom panel is a **distribution of statistics** — one dot per study, not per marble. Click **+1** a few more times to add more studies.

steps.instruction: Now click **+1000** to run a thousand simulated studies quickly and let the null distribution fill in.

requires.hint: Click **+1000** to draw at least 500 samples, then answer below.

steps.observe: Look at the bottom panel and the **SD of p̂'s** readout, then compare it to the theory value **√(p(1−p)/n)**.

gate.question: Where is the null distribution of p̂ centered, and what is its shape?

choices.text: Centered near 0.10 and roughly bell-shaped (with a mild right skew)

gate.feedback: It centers at p = 0.10 (the true rate under H₀). The shape is roughly bell-shaped but with a **mild right skew**: np = 6.2 is below the usual threshold of 10, and p = 0.10 sits close to the floor of 0, so the normal approximation is only approximate here. Your **{{samples}}** studies gave an SD of p̂'s of **{{statSD}}** — very close to the theory value √(p(1−p)/n) = **{{theorySE}}**.
gate.retryFeedback: Look at where the dots pile up relative to the 0.10 line, and whether the shape is mound-shaped or flat.

steps.instruction: Two different things change this picture in two different ways. First click **+1000 again** (more studies, same n). Then change **sample size n to 200** and draw **+1000** — or click **Freeze this distribution to compare** first, then change n, so you can see both at once.

gate.question: Which change made the distribution narrower?
gate.feedback: Only larger n narrows it. More studies just fill in the *same* distribution more smoothly — its spread doesn't change. A larger n produces a *different*, narrower distribution, because √(p(1−p)/n) shrinks as n grows. (A consultant with more surgeries per study would see less sample-to-sample wobble.)
gate.retryFeedback: Compare the frozen n = 62 distribution to the n = 200 one — same center, different width. Then recall what adding more dots at a fixed n did to the width.

steps.instruction: You've built the null distribution of a proportion from scratch. Before you read the summary, put the key ideas in your own words.

prompts.label: How well did each of your three predictions (center, spread, shape) hold up?
Why do more studies fill in the same distribution, while a larger n produces a different (narrower) distribution?
Why does the null distribution having a stable center and spread make the p-value calculation possible?

steps.reveal: The sample proportion p̂ varies from study to study, but predictably: under H₀ its distribution is centered at the true p = 0.10, has standard deviation √(p(1−p)/n), and is approximately normal — here only *roughly*, with a mild right skew, because np = 6.2 falls below about 10. **More studies** sharpen the picture of that distribution, while **a larger n** changes it — shrinking the spread. This null distribution is exactly what we compare the consultant's observed p̂ = 0.048 against to get a p-value.
